results.title: Criteria for research ethics committee review – UKRI
results.content: Researchers, ROs and research ethics committees (RECs) must ensure all proposals that have been recommended for funding by ESRC are appropriately reviewed before the actual research commences. ### Role of a REC A REC should review the research proposal and make a proportionate judgement concerning whether there is an appropriate balance of risks and benefits of the research. RECs should review research proposals in terms of their ethics probity which will include consideration of the design, outputs and proposed conduct of the research. The knowledge and expectations that members of RECs bring to the ethics review of research proposals are fundamental to the way they are reviewing. ### REC decision RECs may give a favourable opinion on the proposal as submitted, give a provisional approval subject to the researcher meeting specified conditions (which may require further review), or reject the proposal on ethics grounds. ### Ongoing review As part of RO governance, RECs should serve to maintain ethics standards throughout the research lifecycle of a project and effectively and rapidly support researchers in resolving ethics issues as they arise. Where a study design is emergent, the REC should agree, with the researchers, procedures for ongoing ethics review (for example through submission of staged ethics applications relating to different aspects of the work, or through a Project Advisory Group). Procedures for reporting to the REC (or a designated sub-committee) any unforeseen events that might challenge the ethical conduct of the research or which might provide grounds for discontinuing the study should be formally agreed with the researchers. Where a REC or a designated sub-committee considers that a monitoring report or ad hoc audit by the RO has raised significant concerns about the ethics in the conduct of the study, it should request a full and detailed account of the research to be submitted for full ethics review conducted by the responsible REC. Where a principal REC or designated sub-committee considers that a study is being conducted in a way which is not in accord with the conditions of its review or in a way which does not appropriately protect the rights, dignity and welfare of research participants, it should initially arrange a meeting of all those concerned with a view to resolving the difficulties.

results.title: Confidential Reporting Channels & Retaliation Risk - Attorney Aaron Hall
results.content: # Confidential Reporting Channels & Retaliation Risk. Confidential reporting channels are essential for enabling employees to report unethical or illegal conduct safely while reducing retaliation risk. * Confidential reporting channels protect whistleblowers’ identities, reducing fear of retaliation and encouraging ethical disclosures. Although organizations implement various mechanisms to address workplace issues, confidential reporting channels remain essential for fostering a safe and transparent environment. The confidentiality importance in these channels lies in their capacity to protect the identity of individuals who report unethical or illegal conduct, thereby encouraging openness without fear of retaliation. When employees disclose wrongdoing or unethical behavior, legal protections are essential to safeguard them from retaliation and ensure the integrity of the reporting process. Furthermore, legal frameworks often mandate confidentiality to prevent the identification of the reporting individual, thereby reducing the risk of retaliation. Although organizations establish confidential reporting channels to protect the identity of whistleblowers, the effectiveness of these mechanisms is contingent upon the perceived trust in anonymity by potential reporters. Numerous individuals who utilize confidential reporting channels experience various forms of retaliation following their disclosures. Organizations must recognize that the presence of retaliation tactics undermines the integrity of confidential reporting channels and discourages future disclosures. The risk of retaliation highlighted in previous discussions underscores the importance of robust measures to protect the identities of individuals utilizing confidential reporting channels. Effective anonymity measures and confidentiality protocols are essential to maintain trust and encourage reporting. Ensuring anonymity and confidentiality not only protects individuals but also enhances the integrity and effectiveness of the reporting system. By embedding accountability into organizational culture, leaders can mitigate retaliation risks and uphold trust in confidential reporting channels. Furthermore, the implementation of preventive measures is essential to mitigate the risk of retaliation and protect individuals who utilize confidential reporting channels. These steps collectively foster an environment where retaliation risks are minimized, and employees feel secure in reporting misconduct, thereby enhancing the integrity and effectiveness of confidential reporting channels. Although establishing confidential reporting channels is essential, fostering an organizational culture rooted in trust and transparency is equally critical to their effectiveness. Therefore, systemic efforts to embed trust and transparency within organizational values are indispensable for the success of confidential reporting systems and the mitigation of retaliation risk.

Identifying and Addressing Retaliation Risks in Ethics Reporting. Identifying and Addressing Retaliation Risks in Ethics Reporting. However, retaliation remains one of the biggest risks in ethics reporting, discouraging employees from speaking up and undermining workplace integrity. ## Understanding Retaliation Risks in Ethics Reporting. According to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), retaliation accounts for nearly 56% of all workplace discrimination chargesfiled in the U.S. The fear of professional repercussions like demotion, exclusion, or termination, will typically prevent many employees from reporting fraud, harassment, or other misconduct. For your organization’s HR professionals, compliance officers, and ethics leaders, mitigating retaliation risks should be critical, and all should act toward maintaining a culture of transparency and trust. An employee with a history of strong performance who suddenly receives negative feedback after filing an ethics report may be experiencing retaliation. Moving an employee to a less desirable role or significantly altering their responsibilities after an ethics complaint can be a form of retaliation, particularly if the change results in career setbacks or reduced job satisfaction. A sudden increase in supervision or micromanagement directed at an employee who recently filed a complaint can be a sign of retaliation. You cannot have a culture of ethics and compliance without a strong anti-retaliation policy, in your firm. Your employees will be more likely to report ethical violations when they trust that their identity will be protected. If an employee or manager is found guilty of retaliation, your organization must swiftly enforce consistent disciplinary actions: from formal warnings to termination. HR and compliance teams should review ethics reports, retaliation claims, and employee feedback to track trends and identify weaknesses in this system. Key indicators such as reporting rates, case resolutions, and employee satisfaction scores can provide insights into the effectiveness of anti-retaliation efforts. A workplace free from retaliation is the first step towards maintaining corporate integrity, legal compliance, and employee trust. But keep in mind that a retaliation-free workplace isn’t just about compliance, it’s about creating an ethical foundation where honesty and accountability thrive.

results.title: Keith Read on Retaliation Risk [Podcast] - The Compliance and Ethics Blog
results.content: Home Compliance Keith Read on Retaliation Risk. # Keith Read on Retaliation Risk [Podcast]. Retaliation is the bane of every compliance program, with the potential of destroying employee confidence in reporting systems, not to mention embarrassing and expensive lawsuits. It is also complex and can be subtle, explains Keith Read, a former chief ethics and compliance officer and author of the book The Unconventional Compliance Officer: Doing Things Differently. But there is also softer, more subtle retaliation, such as not including the whistleblower in meetings or on projects. He advises compliance teams to be sensitive to all of the many forms of retaliation and to treat it  as a risk area. That means look at where and how retaliation can occur, and then take the time to determine if is occurring. He found that retaliation followed certain managers around the organization. Listen in to learn more about how to prevent retaliation from undercutting your compliance program.
